title: Search your files for the minute a podcast mentions sleep
summary: Search your files for the minute a podcast mentions sleep, or the lease clause about pets. DigUp runs EmbeddingGemma 2 on your own machine across photos, PDFs, audio and video, and skips keys and .ssh: https://github.com/ARahim3/DigUp
body_markdown:
Finding a file is hard when you cannot remember its name or an exact word inside it. DigUp, from ARahim3/DigUp, lets you describe what is in the file instead. Type "zebra in a video" and it opens the clip at the moment the zebra shows up. Type "where they talk about sleep" and it jumps to that minute of a podcast. Type "the clause about pets in the lease" and it shows the PDF page.

It does this on your own computer, on a Mac, on Windows or on Linux, with nothing you index leaving the machine.

## One model for text, pictures, audio and video

DigUp is built on EmbeddingGemma 2, the multimodal embedding model Google DeepMind released in October 2026. It places text, images, audio and video in one shared space, so a photo of a dog on a beach lands next to the words "a dog on the beach". It understands more than 100 languages, it is open under Apache 2.0, and at 740M parameters it is small enough for a laptop. That language range means a search in English can find a note written in Bengali or Arabic, and the other way round.

Invoice numbers, error codes and names are also matched exactly as written, in file names and document text, so one search covers both the idea and the string. On a Mac that includes text inside screenshots.

Long media gets handled in windows. The model listens to 30 seconds at a time, so DigUp indexes audio as overlapping 30-second windows and a match points to its moment. Video gets a frame every few seconds, one per shot, plus its soundtrack. PDFs are indexed page by page, scans included, up to 5,000 pages a file.

## What it will not read

Since DigUp indexes your disk, here is what it leaves alone. It reads only the folders you choose. It never reads keys, certificates, password files, hidden folders like `.ssh`, apps or caches. It skips folders that look like datasets, and it never downloads files that only live in the cloud, such as iCloud on a Mac or OneDrive on Windows. It only reads files and never changes, moves or uploads them.

Code is off by default. Outside the folders you pick for code search it never reads code, and inside a code project, meaning a folder with `.git` or `package.json`, it reads only screenshots. Turn code search on for chosen repos and queries like "code: retry a failed call with backoff" find the function whatever it is called.

DigUp goes online to download the model once and to check for updates once a day. The project says that update check sends nothing about your files, and you can turn it off. There is no account and no telemetry. The project also warns that DigUp is published only on its GitHub Releases page and its own site, and that other sites offering it are not the project's.

## The first pass costs time

The model download is 865 MB, once. On a Mac, the first pass takes a few minutes for a few hundred files and can take an hour for a big Downloads folder. On Windows and Linux, DigUp uses the graphics card where that is faster. On a processor alone a picture takes a few seconds, about five on a 2017 laptop's Core i5, so a large photo library can take hours. Setup shows the estimated time for each folder before you commit, measured on your machine. After that, a new file becomes searchable a few seconds after it lands.

## Trying it

The Mac build needs Apple Silicon and macOS 14 or later, and installs from the DMG or with `brew install --cask arahim3/tap/digup`. Windows 10 or 11 and Linux builds are in beta, and the Windows installer is not signed yet. Press Shift+Command+Space on a Mac, or Ctrl+Shift+Space elsewhere, and describe what you want. I would start with one small folder of screenshots and recordings, which a name search handles worst, before pointing it at a whole home directory.
